messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Nun
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Event Site: avoid site of the event, Magical Prevention: perform mental rituals to prevent bad things from happening again, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost
  Memory: Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning, Vivid Memory: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed., Partial Clarity: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Sister Margaret is a 55-year-old woman who has lived in the same Catholic convent for more than two decades, in a rhythm once organized by prayer, communal meals, and visits to the parish school. The event that unsettled that order happened eight months ago, when one of the older sisters, a close friend she had helped care for during a period of declining health, collapsed in a corridor near the small infirmary room. Margaret had been the one to hear the fall. She still remembers the sound of the body hitting the floor and the sight of her friend lying at an angle that immediately felt wrong. Some parts of those minutes are fixed in almost photographic detail—the hem of the sister’s habit twisted beneath her, the smell of floor polish, the cold brightness from the window at the end of the hall—while other moments drop away entirely. She cannot say clearly who called 911 or exactly how long she knelt there, only that she has flashes of pressing at her friend’s shoulder and thinking, with rising panic, that she should have checked on her earlier.

Her account of what happened is saturated with blame. Margaret has come to believe that the death happened because of the way she acted: if she had not delayed, if she had noticed some sign sooner, if she had insisted on more supervision, perhaps her friend would still be alive. What torments her most is the conviction that she failed in a duty that mattered deeply to her, that she should have protected another sister and did not. From there a broader doubt has taken hold. She no longer trusts her own judgment in the simple, ordinary ways she once did; she is certain that when something important depends on her, she will miss what matters. Those beliefs seem to fasten onto the memory itself. The most searing images return with absolute clarity, as if her mind is presenting evidence against her, while the blank stretches feel to her like proof that she cannot even rely on herself to know what happened.

In the months that followed, those memories began arriving without warning. Walking past a polished hallway at the convent, catching the sharp scent of disinfectant outside the infirmary, or hearing a sudden thud during chores could bring back the whole scene instantly, so vividly that for a moment she felt she was back on the floor beside her friend. Because the memory could overtake her so abruptly, she began avoiding the corridor where the collapse occurred, taking a longer route through the building even when it made her late for communal prayer. She also started pulling away from grief reminders more broadly: she leaves quickly if conversation turns to the sister who died, avoids looking at her photograph in the memorial display, and has found reasons not to help sort her belongings. At work in the convent, these maneuvers are now woven into her day so thoroughly that other sisters have noticed how often she volunteers for tasks in distant rooms and declines anything near the infirmary.

Margaret also developed quiet rituals in her head that she does not disclose easily because they feel irrational and shameful. Before bed, before another sister leaves for an appointment, or if an ambulance passes nearby, she repeats set prayers in a particular number and order until it feels “safe enough,” as if failing to do so might allow another catastrophe. These rituals make sense to her because she feels so unable to rely on herself; if her own judgment failed once, she reasons, she must guard against failure in every possible way. Yet the more she depends on these private acts and on steering away from reminders, the more fragile she feels. Each avoided hallway seems to confirm that she cannot bear what happened, and each ritual quietly reinforces the idea that danger will return unless she manages it perfectly.

That pattern has narrowed her world and sharpened the memory rather than softening it. By staying away from the site and from reminders of the sister she lost, she has never had the ordinary repetition that might make the memory feel like something in the past; instead it remains preserved in jagged pieces, either intensely clear or abruptly blank. When it breaks through, it does so with the same force, and Margaret reads that force as further evidence of failure: if she were stronger, if she had done the right thing then and were handling it rightly now, she believes she would not be so vulnerable to it. In turn she doubles down on avoidance and on the mental prayers, trying to prevent another loss and to prevent the memory from taking hold, only to find herself more watchful, more restricted, and less trusting of herself.

Her husband, from whom she has long had a warm but somewhat geographically divided marriage because of religious life and family arrangements, recently told her that every phone call now circles back to the same question of what she should have done differently. What finally brought Margaret to seek help was a recent incident in the convent hallway: a novice dropped a metal tray, and Margaret was instantly back in the moment of finding her friend on the floor. She had to steady herself against the wall, then spent the evening repeating prayers in her room, convinced that something terrible would happen to another sister if she stopped. She comes to treatment frightened that she is becoming someone governed by dread and self-reproach, and hoping, cautiously, that she might learn how to remember her friend without feeling condemned by the memory.
